chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn Ahmad, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Abu Muhammad al-Ansari, from Abdullah ibn Sinan, who said:

I said to Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him): 'A man has dirhams (silver coins) as a debt upon him for me, so he gives me kohl (eye cosmetic).' He (peace be upon him) said: 'Silver is exchanged for silver, and whatever is from kohl is a debt upon him until he returns it to you on the Day of Resurrection.'

key_terms.الدَّرَاهِمُ: Dirhams (silver coins), representing the currency of silver
key_terms.الْفِضَّةُ بِالْفِضَّةِ: Silver for silver, the principle of equal exchange for the same commodity
key_terms.الْمُكْحُلَة: Kohl (eye cosmetic), used here as a commodity distinct from silver
key_terms.دَيْنٌ: Debt, indicating an obligation to repay
key_terms.يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ: The Day of Resurrection, indicating the time of final settlement

ai.seo_question: How is a debt of silver settled if the debtor pays with a different commodity like kohl?
ai.summary: This narration from al-Kafi clarifies the application of *qabd* (possession) in *bay' al-dayn* (sale of debt), establishing that since kohl is not silver, it cannot serve as immediate payment for a silver debt. Instead, the kohl constitutes a new debt (*qard*) that remains outstanding until the Day of Judgment, preventing *riba* (usury) through unequal possession of the specific commodity. This highlights the Shia scholarly emphasis on strict commodity-specificity in debt settlements to ensure fairness and avoid hidden interest.
